Trade and Commerce A commonwealth conference is to be held in September of this year but the minister does not tell the house what the attitude of the government is going to be on that very important proposal put forward by the United Kingdom authorities. Surely if we believe in the parliamentary system at all parliament is entitled to know the policy of the government on this important aspect of our foreign trade. That is particularly so in view of the fact that the present government took office, as they are so fond of saying, for the first time after 22 years in opposition.
Mr. Pallet!: Twenty-two years of no policy.

Twenty-two years that is exactly what I was seeking to say. After 22 years with no policy on the subject the opposition came into power and they now decline to deal with the matter.
Mr. Pallet!: You had better check your answer on that.

The hon. member for Peel has the advantage of sitting very close to the Hansard reporter and he puts interjections on Hansard which it is not always possible to hear. That one I did hear.
I was glad to hear the minister make reference today to the European common market. I hope he will develop that subject a little more because there are many people in this country who fear the direction it may take and who are anxious that the government should co-operate closely in that development to see that it does not take a trend that will be harmful or restrictive so far as the trade of the area with Canada is concerned.
I think probably the aim with respect to it is not objectionable. I am not speaking about the aim or criticizing the minister at the moment, but I wish he would inform us more fully on that subject, just what information he has as to the factors that might affect us favourably and adversely, and the attitude and actions of the government with respect to them.
Then at long last we got a statement from the minister about trade with China. I was particularly interested in that because of the many statements made by the Prime Minister, particularly during the recent election campaign, as well as other supporters of the present government. The Prime Minister's language seemed to indicate an expectation of sharply increased trade with China. I should like to ask the minister if he would clear up in a precise way the exact situation concerning the export to China of materials that might not be considered strategic, in view of the apparent confusion arising out of the attempt to get this information by a

Supply-Trade and Commerce process of questions and answers on orders of the day. This subject is too large, perhaps, to be dealt with properly on orders of the day. There is a great desire to obtain that information.
I would ask him if he would consider working out a precise statement on this subject and putting it on the record during the consideration of these estimates, so we could have it as an authoritative statement as of this date. In this statement I would hope he would clarify the confusion that now exists in connection with Canadian subsidiaries of United States owned companies. The apparent conflict arises because these subsidiaries are subject to Canadian law, but at the same time the United States owners may be subject to United States law. I am aware of the fact it is a subject of some difficulty, but I believe it is a subject on which we should have a precise statement.
On the subject of trade with China, I read with some interest Mr. Forsyth-Smith's article in the publication Foreign Trade. It was a very good article, as far as it went. In view of the minister's statement today about the willingness of Canadian exporters to go abroad in an effort to sell products, and his own interest and statements along that line, would he say whether or not he has in immediate prospect any trade trip to China? There was a small item about that in the newspaper the other day, with which I think he is familiar, indicating that he was going. However, it seemed to me to be one of those vague items that left one in considerable doubt as to whether he was or was not going. I hope he will clear up that point.
I was not quite clear as to the position of our trade commissioners in China. Have we a trade commissioner now in China?
Just in Hong Kong.
Does he cover China?
What is his exact position?
We have a trade commissioner stationed in Hong Kong, Mr. Forsyth-Smith. He spent two weeks in China last fall on invitation of the Chinese government.

Does his territory cover
Hong Kong?

His territory covers Hong
Kong and adjacent countries.
Does it include China?
Yes.

As the minister correctly expected, I have a considerable interest in the subject of trade with the West Indies. As he will have noticed, there is a resolution on the order paper standing in my name which
IMr. Mcllraith.]
deals with the subject of trade with the West Indies. It is not my purpose to elaborate it here, particularly, because I expect that on Monday, or one of the Mondays very shortly, we shall have an opportunity of debating that subject in a specific way. While this will not give an opportunity to ask questions, my remarks could probably be more properly left until that stage.
There is one aspect of this matter, however, arising out of the minister's statement, with which I should like to deal now. He spoke about the importance of this market and the growth of the trade with the West Indies over the last number of years. It has a historic background, and it has a tremendous importance to an area of this country, which I think I can say with propriety needs help in its development at this time to a degree that is equal to or greater than the need of any other part of this country. I refer, of course, to the maritimes.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.

I listened with great interest to the minister's recitation of the activities of his department, the first he has made since he has taken office. While a great deal of what he had to say was informative, I must frankly say it was not inspiring. You know, Mr. Chairman, the minister does not talk like a salesman. I could not imagine anyone selling very much with the minister's approach to this question. He reminded me of the old-fashioned storekeeper who used to sit on an apple box and say, "Come and get it." I was reminded also of an early schoolmaster of mine, nearly 60 years ago, who used to lecture on history. I thought the minister gave us a good lecture on history this afternoon, but I do not think there was very much insight into the future. He did not sound much like a prophet.
I was interested in his reference to trade with the United Kingdom, the European common market, trade with Japan, Latin America and the possibility of developing further trade in the British West Indies. I was interested, too, in his brief and somewhat noncommittal statement with respect to China. The minister stated the trade commissioner learned last fall that the Chinese people were interested in trading with Canada, and in purchasing some of the commodities we have for sale in the export market. I was amazed to hear him say that. You know, Mr. Chairman, we in this group have been trying to tell governments that for five years. The minister has sent a trade commissioner into China surreptitiously, up the

backstairs as it were so they could disown him if he did get into trouble, and he comes back and informs us that there are possibilities of trade. Well, you know, it does me good to repeatedly be able to get up in this house and finally find that the things this group have been saying for years previously have been proven to be correct and have been accepted by the government in power.
Then, coming to British Columbia, I am particularly interested in the problems of trade which affect that province and, more particularly, those which affect my constituency. I do not usually enter into local and parochial matters and things of that sort. However, this is such an important subject that I must deal with one or two matters that concern employers and employees in my constituency. However, I must turn to some capitalist sources to support my arguments on behalf of this group and with respect to surplus commodities we have for sale in Canada. There is no doubt that we have a great deal of surplus commodities in this country at this time. At the same time we have hundreds of thousands of unemployed. I want to deal briefly with some of the things we have in surplus based on information from capitalist sources, strong supporters of free enterprise. Then I want to deal briefly with some of the support for trade with China and the attitude of prominent industrialists and organizations in British Columbia. I am going to deal with this question particularly because while we are all for the development of trade with the other countries that have been mentioned, there are limitations to the possibility of that development. We are moving in that respect into fairly well harrowed fields. We in this group may believe that the greatest possibility for the cultivation of a market in Asia is to a great extent in China. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, on that account I am going to confine my remarks this afternoon to that country.
Before doing so, however, I want to put on the record a few facts which indicate the things we have in surplus in Canada at the present time and the situation with respect to the mining, lumbering and smelting industries and with respect to agriculture. However, I am going to leave the question of dealing with the problems of the lumber industry to another colleague of mine who is also greatly interested in this question, and the problems of the wheat producers and their requirements with respect to the sale of wheat to another colleague of mine, namely the hon. member for Assiniboia who on occasion has been known to rise in his place in this house and have a few words to say on the
Supply-Trade and Commerce marketing of wheat. I now want to quote from the Financial Post of February 15, 1958. That paper has this to say with respect to copper:
It becomes increasingly evident that the copper industry needs an increase in consumption, particularly in North America.
Copper producers are fighting hard to build up demand. Now that they have cut back output by about 10 per cent on a world basis (excluding Russia), they want to improve their markets . . .
Canadian producers are in a difficult position, depending on both the United States and United Kingdom markets since domestic use isn't a vital factor.
They have got to find some other markets than the United Kingdom and the United States before their problems are going to be solved. Then the Financial Post of March 8, 1958, commenting on the copper situation, states:
Canadian copper is largely produced in conjunction with other metals like nickel, lead, zinc and gold. It is difficult to reduce production of copper since often the "other" metal is the one sought and copper is the byproduct.
That is the situation that exists in British Columbia in a number of mines.
Thus Canadian mines-ranking fourth as suppliers-so far have largely been forced to ride along the bumps of the confused world copper picture. They could not readily reduce production, conserve ore and generally pull in their belts.
Instead they have had to go on producing the metal ... at substantially reduced prices.
Then, Mr. Chairman, I want to deal briefly with the comments of the Financial Post with respect to the situation concerning the marketing of lead and zinc. The Financial Post of March 8, 1958 comments as follows on the lead and zinc situation, and this is an extremely important question to the mining fraternity, both employers and employees in British Columbia:
Lead and zinc are among Canada's troubled minerals. They are riding out the storm of falling prices that also hit copper, and the general slump in lead and zinc business occurred for the same basic reason as in the case of copper-an oversupply of metal in relation to the market . . .
The world squeeze out in the two metals resulted in some casualties in Canada. In British Columbia, giant Consolidated Mining and Smelting closed down two mines. Galkeno Mines in the Mayo district in the Yukon suspended operations. Consolidated Sudbury Basin, a potential supplier of lead and zinc, cancelled its plans to get into production.
The same Financial Post notes as follows:
It is estimated that some 68 per cent of Canada's zinc production is sold in the United States and some 25 per cent of lead.
Then the Financial Post deals with the wheat situation and gives an analysis of it but I am going to leave that question to the hon. member for Assiniboia. Then we come to the question of lumber and fertilizers. This

Supply-Trade and Commerce is what Canadian Business Week of October, 1957 has to say:
Canada, again remembers its best pre-war Asian customer. In the late twenties, this country shipped as much as $29 million worth of B.C. lumber annually to China. This is a market which the depression, World War II and post-war ideological divisions have completely dried up. Today, with the B.C. coast lumber industry in the worst slump since the depression-bound thirties, the cry has gone up from several senior west coast lumber company executives that China should no longer be excluded as a trading partner of Canada.
The article goes on to say this:
"It's the only fresh lumber market left", said one of them last spring ...
During the last 18 months, senior Canadian and American businessmen, including Henry Ford II, Canadian-born multi-millionaire Cyrus Eaton, H. E. MacMillan, chairman of the board of Vancouver's MacMillan and Bloedel Ltd., and James S. Duncan, OBE, former president of world-selling Massey-Harris-Ferguson Ltd., have all come out for a realistic Red China trading policy. Last January, Ford called for a 'realistic decision' where China is concerned and Eaton warned the western powers to 'stop goading Red China'-
Then the article goes on further to say this:
The largest market on earth, perhaps already overcommitted to the Russian economy for industrial heavy equipment and to a limited degree for consumer goods, is virtually closed to the products of the west in any volume. Before it's too late and before it forgets what it once could buy from us, China's traditional consumer goods trade with us must be restored, say western businessmen and manufacturers.
Then in my few brief remarks I want to quote some statements favouring trade with China which now rise on every hand. Mr. W. C. Mainwaring, vice president, British Columbia Electric Co., Vancouver, B.C., had this to say:
Canada's exports to China dropped from $37 million in 1947 to $1 million in 1954 . . . there is every indication that China has dollars to pay for increased trade with Canada-
Mr. C. M. Forsyth-Smith, Canadian trade commissioner in Hong Kong had this to say: There is a "promising market" in Red China for Canadian goods-
Hon. Earle Westwood, British Columbia provincial minister of trade and industry Victoria, had this to say:
The Chinese demand for fertilizer is so great that the annual requirements for the Shanghai area alone would absorb the total production of the Trail plant of Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company.
Yet here we are having to cut back production and men are being laid off while we have this large potential market for fertilizer and that fertilizer is badly needed in the Asiatic countries and in China.
Then again, Mr. Chairman, there is another statement I wish to quote. I may say that I am just summarizing and more or less taking statements from here and there so as not [Mr. Herridge.l
to take up the time of the committee unduly in quoting these capitalist authorities to support the arguments we have made in this house for a period of five years. I have here in my hand a page from the Montreal Gazette of June 28. In it there is an article which is headed "Canada Losing 'Legitimate' Trade; Muir Finds Others Grab China Market". I just want to quote Mr. Muir briefly. In this article Mr. Muir is quoted as saying this:
"It was galling to meet (in China) and to talk with the selling forces of other Western powers, not only obviously getting business but enthusiastic about it, while our people seem to sit back and wait for a silver platter deal,"-
By our people he means the exporters of Canada and this government. He goes on to say:
The Canadian government should see to it that, "if any Canadian enterprise should be induced by outside influence to deviate from its responsibility to the Canadian worker and the Canadian economy by declining legitimate and clean business, drastic and immediate steps should be taken to discipline it"-
The minister sent a trade commissioner to China last fall and he informs the house this morning very briefly and in modest and mild tones and terms that there are "some possibilities" with respect to a market in China. I think it is obvious, however, that the leading industrialists in this country and the organizations to which they belong are not satisfied that this government is moving fast enough in this direction in order to take advantage of this great potential market. In concluding my references to these persons I wish to quote a resolution passed by the British Columbia chamber of commerce at its recent meeting in Vancouver which clearly indicates that this chamber of commerce was not satisfied with the government's policies in this respect, otherwise they would not have passed a resolution in these terms. This resolution was, I am informed, adopted unanimously and reads as follows:
Whereas Canada's volume of international trade is of vital concern to the economic welfare of all Canadians; and
Whereas the diversified product of its natural resource industries requires that trade should be conducted on a multilateral basis; and
Whereas exchange of trade and closer persona] relationships are an essential factor for the development of international understanding and goodwill;
Therefore be it resolved that the British Columbia Chamber of Commerce urge upon the federal government the need for establishing trade relations with communist China, subject to the imposition of such conditions as would safeguard the movement of strategic materials.
It is obvious from that resolution that the British Columbia chamber of commerce is not satisfied with the actions taken by the government to date with respect to the development of trade with red China. Why

did they take that view? Because that convention would have been attended by a large number of men interested in the primary industries of British Columbia and would have surpluses to sell.
Another thing to which I wish to draw the attention of the minister is the fact that in that resolution are the words "closer personal relationships". It is quite obvious from those words that they do not consider the sending of a trade commissioner to Hong Kong a close enough personal relationship. As I and others in this group have said before, we believe that such a close personal relationship can only be realized by the recognition by this government of red China. In doing so we do not recognize a system; we do not agree with their policies, but we cannot expect a great nation like that, with a population of over 600 million, to carry on a satisfactory trade relationship unless we recognize the government of that country. We do hope, therefore, that the Canadian government will cease riding on the coat tails of Mr. Dulles and will show a little courage and do what the majority of the Canadian people want them to do, that is, first to recognize China and, secondly, to take a much more positive approach to the development of this great market which would, without doubt, provide an immense outlet for our surplus commodities and employment for many persons who are now unemployed in this country.
It is quite obvious that the, shall I say, snail's pace which the government is adopting with respect to this matter at the present time is unsatisfactory to the industrialists and to their employees both capital and labour in British Columbia having expressed their discontent and their opinions in various ways. I do urge the minister to recognize the feeling in the country. I think the government and possibly the minister himself are somewhat out of touch, particularly with the feeling in British Columbia, with respect to the development of trade in Asia, recognition of red China and the development of trade with this great country.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to take a few moments to address the house. It is rather unfortunate that I should follow the hon. member for Kootenay West because my subject is very much the same as his. I do not agree with his contention that the government is out of step with public thinking on this matter; I believe the government has moved faster and with more effect than any other government has done, and in this respect I would like to quote a few figures.
Canadian exports to China in the first five months of this year totalled $2.75 million, whereas in previous years Canadian exports, firstly in 1954, totalled $70,000, while in 1955
Supply-Trade and Commerce they totalled approximately $1 million, in 1956 $2,400,000 and in 1957 about $1,400,000. So that if the rate of exports is kept up during the balance of the year we will export to China this year as much as we have exported in the preceding four years. In addition to this, the government has sent a trade commissioner to China and has taken action in consultation with the United States with a view to freeing trade with China. During the consultations which the minister and the Prime Minister had with the President of the United States, as we have been advised through press reports and in other ways, steps were agreed upon so that this trade can be made open to us on the same basis as it is available to other NATO countries. I think that is a pretty good record and, coming from British Columbia, I do not minimize the value of trade with China. I know how important it is not only to British Columbia but to all of western Canada.
I would like to refer to the trade pattern in the United Kingdom since that country recognized China. The U.K. recognized red China on January 6, 1950, and in that year trade with China totalled approximately $10 million; it dropped by over a quarter in 1951, came back to $12 million in 1952 and from that point on it has steadily risen to a total export trade of $34 million approximately in 1957. United Kingdom imports from China have followed pretty much the same pattern and stand at close to $40 million in 1957.
This is a sizeable trade picture but we should not inflate the importance of it in regard to United Kingdom trade or trade with other countries. The value of trade with China is in its future potential, in that this is a pattern of increasing trade which will rise at a very fast rate from year to year with the development of that country through industrialization and through the measures which its government has been taking to increase living standards which, even now, are fantastically low compared with our own.
The hon. member for Kootenay West has quoted rather extensively from the report of Mr. James Muir, the chairman and president of the Royal Bank of Canada, and I must say that the statement of a leading businessman such as Mr. Muir must not be ignored. I believe that Mr. Muir has helped to correct some of the misconceptions we perhaps have had as a result of previous reports of activity in red China. I do think, however, in respect of his remarks about the exporting fraternity who, he says, should shake themselves, should get busy and should visit China either individually or as a group and keep at this job in order to develop trade, what the government has done and is doing had to be done first. Hon. members know that there is an

Supply-Trade and Commerce embargo on certain goods and that CONCOM, a subcommittee of NATO, has been sitting in Europe and has brought the strategic control lists in regard to the U.S.S.R. and China into a state of conformity. A great many articles and commodities which were formerly embargoed have now been freed from that list.
The trouble with our industrial setup is that the United States has taken the stand that it will not trade with red China and that that decision of the United States government will apply to the operations of United States plants in other countries. Because approximately 60 per cent of the industrial capacity of Canada is controlled from the United States we cannot establish free channels through Hong Kong for material and commodities for sale to red China. This does not assist us in respect to those industries which are in the main under United States control or ownership. That is the reason why the recent meeting between the President of the United States and the government of Canada is of such importance because it frees these channels of trade so we can participate in trade with China on somewhat the same basis as the United Kingdom. If it works out as it is supposed to we should see an increase in trade with China.
There are a couple of questions I should like to ask the minister in regard to the new trade pattern and they relate to how the setup will work. Will a China trade section be established in the Department of Trade and Commerce? It would seem inconceivable to me that a Canadian company subject to United States regulations because of ownership should have to go through the U.S. state department for a permit or relaxation of regulations allowing it to make shipments to China. I would think the way it should be handled would be for the company to go to some section of the Department of Trade and Commerce which would have clear lines of communication with the proper officials in Washington so that an answer could be given in a relatively short time. I can see businessmen going grey with frustration if they have to wade through the intricacies of the United States state department in order to secure a permit to make a shipment. If a China trade section is established in our own Department of Trade and Commerce the headquarters should be located at Vancouver and this should work out very well.
I have been told that within the past few weeks agents have tried to buy quantities of bleached sulphite pulp for shipment to China but have not been successful. This commodity is produced only in mills on the coast that are United States-owned. The question I have is this. To whom should the agent

go if he wished to get clearance to make a deal with Rayonier or Crown Zellerbach, subsidiaries or whatever company it might be, to get that trade moving?
In conclusion I simply wish to reiterate that it is easy enough to criticize in these matters. In working out relationships such as these, and particularly with the United States, and in setting up a Canadian agency in Hong Kong to make contacts with a government which at the present time we cannot recognize, a considerable amount of work and planning is involved. To my way of thinking the record speaks for itself and indicates that the government is working along lines which will give us a fair share of the China market in the future.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if I could direct a question to the hon. member who has just spoken? If I understood him correctly, the hon. gentleman said that we cannot at the present time recognize China. Would the hon. member care to elaborate and say why we cannot?
No.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a moment or two of the committee's time in order to complete two points that I had not concluded when my allowance of time expired earlier in this debate this afternoon.
I was speaking near the conclusion of my remarks about the minister's statement with respect to West Indies trade. I agreed with him about the importance of that subject and made reference to the fact that I have a notice of motion standing in my name on the order paper dealing with this subject and that I proposed to make my main remarks pertaining to it on that occasion.
I did, however, want to say something about the minister's remarks in this connection which were important for two reasons. He outlined the historical development of that trade, told of its growth and stressed its importance but he did not elaborate on the policy with respect to the development of our trade with that area. I had hoped he would do so not only because of the general importance of the subject but because of its particular importance to the maritime region.
The one point I want to make clear is the significance of his omission to deal with Canada's part in that trade. We have a trade agreement dating back to the twenties and have participated in the West Indies trade liberalization program. The minister mentioned those things but did not mention the one really significant step we have taken since the government of which he is a

member took office and that is the withdrawal of the tremendous aid we have been giving that area through providing shipping for the major part of the trade between Canada and that country. It did not apply to bauxite and certain items of that nature. I refer specifically to the Canadian National Steamships vessels which operated for years.
It is perfectly true that they were not operating at a profit and had to be subsidized. If I remember correctly the Minister of Transport said that the subsidy we were paying was $200,000 a year and that it would rise to double that amount this year. I have not checked that figure today and stand to be corrected by the minister if I have misquoted the facts. But the real crux of the matter is this. As was stated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Federation of the West Indies has just come into being. They are encountering all the difficulties inherent in a country achieving a new status and entering a new period of development. At that strategic moment in the development of that area Canada discontinued the one form of aid it had been giving the West Indies. No satisfactory explanation was given in this house for the discontinuance of the aid when the Minister of Transport discussed the withdrawal of the Canadian National Steamships service and no reference was made to it whatever today by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I respectfully suggest that it is of such importance to the trade to warrant better treatment than that. Many people in this country hold the view that this action was taken without mature and careful consideration.
It may well have been that as time went on something different would have had to be done about the arrangements than was being done but surely the time to take the decision to discontinue that service and sell the ships was not at this period in the history of the development of that area. Canada is providing a new ship which is now under construction, I believe, for trade within that area but while it is needed and represents a good gesture it is as nothing compared with the foreign trade aspect of shipping being serviced by the Canadian National Steamships lines.
In the relationship to trade this is not a subject that should be brushed aside. I have the strongest condemnation of the government for their arbitrary action. When the Minister of Transport was dealing with this-and I wish he were here now so that he could answer these remarks-I rather got the impression that he lost his patience rather quickly because of some labour difficulties that management of the steamship company were having at the time and he 57071-3-148

Trade and Commerce took precipitate action which the facts did not warrant. I rather got the impression, due to his characteristics in answering the questions that were put to him, that he did not adequately consider the question of disposal of those ships and the method of disposal, to what area they would be sent, and so on. I do not know whether he considered the question of disposal of them to the West Indies federation, or to any of the component parts of the federation, or even the gift of one of them to the federation or to one of the component parts of the federation.
The other point I wanted to deal with very briefly was the minister's remarks pertaining to the balance of trade and the figures he quoted with apparent satisfaction. He gave the figures of exports to the United States. Our exports to the United States were down in May a bit. He spoke about that subject. There is a problem of imbalance of payments between Canada and the United States. He dealt with the imbalance of commodity figures-trade-between Canada and the United States. But one very significant factor in what he quoted is the apparent improvement, in that he said there was a lessening of the deficit, and that is this. If he will analyse figures he will find that one of the reasons for that apparent improvement, or what I took from his remarks on trade as an improvement, is the sharp decline in the import of heavy capital goods to develop this country. The reason for that sharp decline in the imports of heavy capital goods is that we in this country, unfortunately, are suffering a business recession and the development that we would all wish to see going on, requiring heavy industrial machinery and the like, is not going on. To quote figures, to refer to that fact in a way that would indicate approval is to do something that is regrettable or, should I say, not to quote the figures, to omit to quote them, is to do something that is unfortunate.
Then there was another aspect of the matter of balance of trade that concerned me. The minister, when he spoke, made reference to the exports to the United Kingdom and to the commonwealth, and so on. There was the question of the exports to Asia and to India in particular. The regular exports of wheat, and the exports of wheat under the Colombo plan and the exports under that special agreement where there was a loan providing for repayment over a seven-year period were a substantial factor but it is quite wrong, Mr. Chairman, to mix up the problem the country faces concerning balance of payments with the difference in exports and imports in commodity trade figures and
2338	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce use the two terms as if they were synonymous because the Colombo plan figures show in the wheat aspect as exports but there is no payment in cash. That is a contribution properly made by the taxpayers of this country for a very laudable purpose and objective. It should not be lost sight of when one is speaking about the difficulties we have in the balance of payments, and the same thing goes, to a lesser extent, with these figures where the trade is financed by long-term loans.
Incidentally, there was another matter in using the wheat figures and I wish the minister had gone a little farther and completed the subject. There was the matter of the export of wheat to Russia, which was reflected in this year's figures. As I understand it, the export of wheat to Russia was under a 3-year agreement. I believe that the
1957	portion was not taken but is in the
1958	figures. If we are to discuss wheat exports intelligently those factors have to be acknowledged and dealt with. Wheat export is of tremendous significance to the economy of this country and I would hope that in its discussion those aspects could be brought forward fully and completely. Because shipments are made at a certain time under a certain laudable aid program and show in the export figures, that figure should not be used as an argument in dealing with the balance of payments problem which is another very real problem we have to face.
I will not encroach on the time of the committee further at this time. I am grateful to the committee for hearing me so soon after my earlier remarks, but I did want to complete that portion of my remarks at an early stage because they related directly to the minister's statement.

Mr. Chairman, I want to talk about the trade in one particular commodity, but before doing so I should like to say how heartily I agree with the hon. member for Ottawa West in welcoming the omission in the statement of the minister of any reference to trade diversion. I hope we have heard the last of that fallacy and I believe it will be remembered in history as the great diversion which became the great deception.
The commodity that I want to talk about is fish, and particularly salt codfish. In his statement the minister passed rather lightly over the difficulties being experienced by the salt codfish industry at the present time. I want to be quite fair. The minister did say difficulties were being experienced but he expressed the hope-which he has expressed before during this session-that


those difficulties would be overcome. However, the minister gave us no information as to any plans he had for overcoming them, nor did he give any real appreciation of the vital importance of this particular export which is, of course, the oldest of all our exports and which I believe is still, so far as the proportion of the total production which has to be exported if there is to be found any market for it at all, one of those which enters most largely into world trade.
I do remember being somewhat surprised about 20 years ago when I first came to Ottawa from Manitoba and first began to hear about salt codfish when someone from the maritime provinces pointed out that in the old Canada before 1949 the proportion of salt codfish exported to the total production was exactly the same as it was of wheat. Of course, now that Newfoundland is a part of Canada the proportion of salt codfish which has to find a market abroad if it is to find any market at all is much higher than the proportion of wheat. Salt codfish to many parts of the Atlantic provinces is every bit as important as wheat is to western Canada, and I am sure the minister will agree with that view.
But we have had very little evidence so far in the house that the government has taken action consonant with the importance of the codfish industry to a very considerable section of the country. I remember I read with some surprise in the St. John's News of July 8, 1957, just over a year ago, the first statement about the famous diversion policy that the Prime Minister made when he came from his aircraft to the press gallery without previously consulting his colleagues on his return from the United Kingdom, a statement which I think will rank in history as one of the most foolish statements ever made by a Canadian prime minister.
In the course of that interview, as reported in the Canadian Press dispatch which appeared in the St. John's News, the Prime Minister was being asked some questions about the proposed British adhesion to a free trade area which would surround the European common market which had, at that time, just been agreed upon by six European nations. I quote part of the article as it appeared in the paper:
Discussing Britain's participation in the proposed European free market, Mr. Diefenbaker said Canada would take a "benevolent" view of this so long as commonwealth farm products were not included. He added that Britain also is inclined this way, though some of the continental countries are not, and that the U.K. realizes such inclusion would be serious not only for Canada but also for Australia and New Zealand. He was asked whether he

would include fish in the commodities that should be excluded. ''I don't think that's a very serious matter," he said.
I know that the Prime Minister did not mean, and I do not want to misrepresent him by suggesting he meant that he did not think fish was a very serious matter. What he meant was that he did not think fish was a very serious matter in relation to the proposed European free trade area. That is a view with which I cannot agree and I certainly hope that the Minister of Trade and Commerce will tell us before the debate closes on his estimates that he does not agree with it either.
The common market, as the minister very well knows, includes France and Italy and, as the minister also knows, France has a base for its salt codfish production in North America in the islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon. Now that there is to be a common market between France and Italy and certain other European countries there will, of course, be a common tariff and the difficulties we have experienced over the years in disposing in Italy of a proportion of our Newfoundland salt fish production are likely to be increased if the greatest care, forethought and attention are not given to every aspect of this problem by the government at all times. That is why-I do not intend to transgress the rules by debating this now; I merely point it out-we on this side of the house were so shocked when the Minister of Finance announced the other day in his budget that he was hoping to negotiate with GATT to increase the most favoured nation tariff on woollen cloth.
Woollen cloth has become one of the increasingly important exports from Italy which is, of course, one of our best customers not only for fish but also for wheat, flour and a considerable number of other products. It is also a country where we sell a great deal more than we buy. We do not feel, particularly at this time, when, because of the common market, the Italian market for fish needs to be safeguarded more jealously and carefully than ever, that anything should be done by the government to affect the exports of Italy to Canada which might invite retaliation or the possibility of retaliation. I can assure the minister that all of us who represent fishing constituencies in eastern Canada will feel very apprehensive about this aspect of that particular situation.
I read yesterday in the St. John's Telegram of July 9 that NAFEL, the sales agency for Newfoundland salt fish, had signed a contract for the sale of 40,000 quintals of salt codfish to Italy this year which is the same quantity as was sold last year. The article goes on to point out that it is very important 57071-3-148J
Supply-Trade and Commerce that fishermen should deliver fish of Italian quality and in sufficient quantity early enough to make possible a shipment to Italy in August. There were certain unfortunate events, of which I am sure the minister is aware, in connection with our shipments to Italy last year which no one wants to see repeated this year.
It is true, because the fishermen are no longer making fish themselves in the quantities they used to make it and more and more of it is being sold to fish plants that the amount of fish of the quality required in the Italian market has been decreasing. The more it decreases and the more fish of a quality which has to be sold in the Caribbean market is produced in its stead the greater are the difficulties of selling our fish and the greater is the possibility of having overhanging the market a surplus of the kind of fish that can be sold in the West Indies but cannot be sold in Europe, together with a shortage of fish to satisfy the European market.
I know it is not directly the problem of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, because of the peculiar division of responsibilities we have in this field, to provide incentives for the production of the kind of article we have to sell. That is his responsibility in the case of wheat; it is not in the case of fish. But I would urge the minister, and I intend on an appropriate occasion to urge the Minister of Fisheries too, to urge his colleagues to consider very carefully whether it would not be in the over-all interests of our fish exports to consider for a few years at least incentive payments for the kind of fish which will satisfy the Italian and Spanish markets until such time as that quality of fish can be produced efficiently and economically in the fish plants so that we will not lose these markets, so that we will tide ourselves over this period of transition with which I am sure the minister is familiar.
There was another very serious blow to our fish exports this year of which, of course, the minister is thoroughly aware. As long ago as November 8 in the last parliament the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo asked the minister about this matter and at that time the minister expressed the hope that something could be done to avert the loss of the Jamaican market. Unhappily the minister was not successful in his efforts and we have lost that market completely for the six months which began on July 1 of this year. We have lost it because the Icelanders have underbid us in that market.
I am not sure whether or not the minister is familiar with the degree to which the Icelandic production is subsidized. It is subsidized at a rate which it is hard to believe

Supply-Trade and Commerce a country as small and as lacking in material wealth as Iceland is, could possibly carry on for any considerable length of time. But the fact remains that the loss of the Jamaican market, which has been one of the best and most stable markets for Newfoundland fish since time immemorial, is a very serious blow to the whole industry. The loss of this market is the result of non-economic competition of a character at least as objectionable as the competition from another country in the wheat market, to which hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches have taken such strong exception in times past.
I do suggest to the minister that, if it is necessary to do so, extraordinary means should be adopted by the government to recover this market. If it is not recovered, if the Canadian producers of salt codfish have to try to find a market in the remaining Caribbean areas, then the results will be serious because we are having to meet subsidized competition from France and Norway in particular in those markets. As the minister knows, for many years we have not been able, because of currency restrictions and exchange controls that he mentioned, to sell fish in Brazil or the other places. The minister indicated another effort was being made to get back into that market. I wish him every success in this effort.
The fact of the matter is that in this salt fish industry, because of the current high levels of unemployment in the Atlantic provinces and because also of the action of the previous administration in inaugurating unemployment insurance for fishermen, we have had a considerable number of men return to the fishing industry. It is estimated that in Newfoundland perhaps 2,000 additional fishermen are engaged in this industry this year. It is of the utmost importance, if the industry is not to face a very serious condition with a very large surplus overhanging the market, that something be done not merely to hold the markets we have but to recover the market in Jamaica and to get back, if we possibly can, into the market in Brazil. Above all, everything should be done to hold and expand the more lucrative European market.
It is for the purpose of drawing to the attention not merely of the minister and the government but of all hon. members, the plight of this industry, the oldest industry in our country, that I speak at this time.
This industry does not rank as high as many others in total monetary value of exports, but it is fair to say that for every thousand dollars of exports more employment is probably created by this industry than any other industry that we have in the country.


A special effort should be made to meet the big problems which this industry faces. One of those problems, as the minister knows, is that the price which is received for fish is set in a world market. There is no way in which the fishermen can get any protection, and yet for most of the things our fishermen have to buy, they not only have to pay the price of goods produced in a protected market but in many cases the price of goods that are produced in the central part of Canada which, in many cases, is higher than the price of those goods in the markets in central Canada. I am sure the minister is very familiar with this argument, coming as he does from the part of the country in which he and I lived for so long.
The minister said he hoped we could get back into the Jamaican market if we could meet the prices which our competitors might be willing to quote in that market. It may be that we will not be able to meet those prices any better on the 1st of January than we were on the 1st of July, not because our fishermen are not producing as efficiently as they could, not because we are not trying to cut costs wherever we can, but because the government of another country is subsidizing the exports, as is certainly the case now with Icelandic exports to Jamaica. As the minister knows, we in Canada are a very considerable customer of Jamaica. I should be very surprised indeed if the people of Iceland provide a very large market for Jamaica. It does seem to me, and I am not suggesting any kind of threat or anything of that sort, that this is a rather powerful argument for the minister's officials to use in any discussions of this subject in the West Indies.
I think some of us, on this side of the house at least, will have something more to say about this subject when the motion standing in the name of the hon. member for Ottawa West comes up for debate, we hope next Monday. In the meantime, I wanted to bring the minister's attention to this problem as forcibly as I could. This minister said, quite correctly, that the market was very good at the moment for fresh and frozen fish. Experience tells us this condition will be influenced by the price of meat generally, but the price of beef particularly. I am told by people with long experience in the fish trade that when the price of beef goes up, the market for fish rises. If the price of beef falls, the market for fish generally falls too, in areas like the United States where consumers can readily shift from one product to another. I think all of us, not only the members from the Atlantic provinces and the minister himself, but from the greater part of Canada, are very apprehensive about that question, the shortage of fodder in western

Canada; the danger of mass sellings and mass slaughterings of cattle, and the danger to our cattle trade. I would add thereby also to our fresh fish exporters. Then again, if the quantity of fresh and frozen fish we could export declined, there would be that much more pressure on the salt fish market.
All of these things are tied together. I do hope the minister will use his influence with his colleagues, and I am sure he will in this case, to take every precaution, including if necessary increasing our imports from the United States, in order to assure an adequate supply of fodder so we can maintain our cattle, maintain orderly markets for cattle in the United States which are important, not only to the farmers who produce cattle but also to the fishermen who sell fish in the United States.

Mr. Chairman, living as I do almost 1,000 miles from the sea, I could certainly not claim to be a salt water fisherman or know too much about codfish in general. However, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks made by my colleague the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, and listened to him point out the danger to the fishing industry on the east coast of Canada. It so happens that the other day I did receive a little bit of detailed information on the trade between this country and Italy and it seems to fit right in now. I think it might be interesting to consider that the deficit of Italy in her trading balance with Canada appears to be steadily growing and that certainly is not what we desire if we wish to increase our trade with all nations, as the minister so ably outlined this afternoon.
But there is great concern, I know from the correspondence I have received, in Italy at this steadily growing imbalance of trade between Italy and Canada. For example, it has increased from $9.1 million in 1955 to $12.8 million in 1956 to $16.1 million in the first half of 1957 and I suppose that as of the present the imbalance of trade between the two countries is even greater. This growing imbalance of trade between the two countries is causing a great deal of concern in Italy itself. In fact, my correspondence indicates to me that they are considerably disturbed about the protectionist tendencies that this present government seems to be formulating in its general trade policies. This is being given considerable display in the trade papers in Italy itself. I am advised that it would hardly be surprising if this did not lead to a reappraisal of Italian policy concerning Canadian imports, especially with respect to the import of codfish. That is all I want to say on that point at the moment.
What I should like to bring to the attention of the minister is a subject which he, for one
Supply-Trade and Commerce reason or another, did not include in his speech. I am very glad that at long last he has decided to make a report to parliament. I believe this is the first one since the present government took office some time ago. In any event, if you will refer to the throne speech given on May 12 of this year, you will see that in one paragraph it refers to small business and states as follows:
In order to assist small business, there will be established a small business section within the administrative machinery of government. The functions of this organization will be to provide liaison between the government and small businesses, to study the problems of small business and to advise on measures necessary to meet them.
The Minister of Justice on June 11 of this year was speaking to the retail merchants association of Canada at Vancouver and a report published in the Toronto Telegram of June 11 reads:
Justice Minister Fulton has outlined to retailers federal plans to help small businessmen solve their problems.
Then it goes on further to say he was speaking to the Retail Merchants Association of Canada and that he said:
-the government is proceeding "at once" to set up a small business section in government.
And so on and so forth.
Mr. Fulton said the government's new section will provide a liaison between government and business and recommend measures to help small businesses including the terms of a loan fund.
If we go back to some of the promises that were made by the Prime Minister in the recent campaign-and I am dealing only with the recent campaign, not the first so-called campaign-we find that according to a Canadian Press dispatch in the Montreal Star of March 18, 1958, the Prime Minister speaking at Selkirk, Manitoba, on March 17 last said the government would set up a special branch to help small business obtain a fair share of government contracts and financial aid to expand.
There was no mention of any particular measure which the present government proposes to take with regard to assisting small business and certainly not with regard to giving any financial assistance. Yet that was one of their major points; and certainly according to the evidence that we have, and according to the minister's own statements on various occasions, I believe that small business accounts for about 50 per cent of domestic trade in this country. If that is true, it seems to me that now is the time for the government to live up to its promises with regard not only to acting as a liaison between small business and government-I am not suggesting that the government indulge in wholesale handing out of contracts except by

Supply-Trade and Commerce tender-but to advancing some proposal as it promised to assist financially small business.
As we well know, the previous government set up a small business department. I believe it was started under the department of reconstruction many years ago and it has been of material assistance to small business throughout Canada by the providing of information, by bringing people together and by assisting generally small businessmen who wanted to make an approach to government and who wanted to get certain research facilities without being obliged to go to the considerable expense of doing the research themselves. So I ask the minister what about this pledge given to the people of this country in the throne speech. What does his department propose to do with regard to assisting small business in his country? There will be ample opportunity, I hope, to ask various leading questions of the minister in an effort to try to get some information which is not necessarily political in character but is with regard to trade itself.
We have heard ad nauseam this proposal to divert 15 per cent of Canada's trade from the United States to the United Kingdom and it has been expanded into an expansion of or increase in export trade for this country; but the basic fact remains that the statement was made that this government proposes to divert 15 per cent of our trade with the United States to the United Kingdom or in other words $650 million per year. That is a disturbing statement or a disturbing fact, if it is true. If it is not true, I think the time has come to deny it once for all. Certainly the minister's words were these, as I took them down today, when he said that what we want is diversification-of course we do-because it will mean a better balance of trade-of course it will. He says we want expansion of foreign trade, that we want to co-operate with all, and that we want to remove discrimination. Yet at the same tune when we hear rumours throughout of a proposed imposition of a dumping proposal, needless to say traders and businessmen in this country are considerably disturbed.
We have dealt with the question of trade with Canada and the United States at some length on other occasions; 70 per cent of our imports from the United States, 60 per cent of our exports to the United States with a deficit of $1,001,000,000. But the minister in a statement given to the Boston Post, I think it was, said that in spite of our desire to diversify our trade, we must do nothing to lessen the over-all total. As I say, this ridiculous suggestion of diverting trade from one country to another, when we as the fourth

trading nation in the world should be bending every effort to expand our trade, should be scotched once for all.
Frequently in this house we have heard the suggestion advanced by the present government that trade should be decentralized from the central provinces to the west and to the east. Has the minister anything to say with regard to that proposal? Has he any policy to advocate in that regard? We also heard a great deal about the trade mission to Britain and all of us wish to increase trade with Great Britain. I hope no one will misunderstand me on that score.
We have, however, received no report from the minister himself in this particular respect. We have had a mission sent over to England, which mission has submitted its report, and that report is very interesting. Under heading No. 6 of the conclusions of the report, "factors affecting British trade in Canada" it refers to the proposal of protection. This is in the last paragraph, namely No. 24, and it says that undoubtedly a number of United Kingdom manufacturers are uneasy about dumping regulations and fair market value and that some do not entirely appreciate the procedures involved.
What we want to know is how the minister is able to get on his feet in this house and propose that we must take every possible step to increase trade with other countries, and at the same time talk about diverting trade from the United States to the United Kingdom, and also at the same time imply that there may be levied subsequently certain dumping duties which, as anyone knows, will only bring about a measure of restriction to trade and will do nothing to increase trade with other countries. We think we should have an explanation of the present government's policy from the minister at this time.
The minister himself referred to the necessity for exhibitions and how they have brought Canadian goods to the attention of foreign purchasers. I am assuming the minister has already visited the Canadian exhibition at the current Brussels trade fair and I think the time has come for him to tell us something about his impressions of our exhibit at that fair. My own opinion is that we ought to go into the fair business on a much larger scale, that it is a measure used by European traders to display their goods and to procure contracts for trade between themselves and other countries. I believe we are lagging in this respect and, as I say, I would like to hear the minister's impressions of our exhibit at Brussels.
There are many other things which I propose to raise in due course but at the present time I wish to thank the minister for having, at long last, brought down a report on his

department and I wish to state that I hope before long he will outline his policy so that the businessmen of our country may know in which direction we are going.

There is just one question I would like to raise in view of the remarks of the hon. member for Ottawa West. I would like the minister to comment on articles which have appeared recently in Montreal newspapers to the effect that oil refineries established in Montreal for some years, having spent millions of dollars to expand the industry in that area, are being forced to go west in order to gain supplies of crude oil. Would the minister also explain how this movement of the oil refineries from the city of Montreal and area will help to solve the acute unemployment problem which exists in that metropolis and will improve the declining economic situation?

Mr. Chairman, in reply to the hon. member, this is not a subject which is of immediate concern to the Department of Trade and Commerce. We are dealing with estimates and I have no supervision over the oil refineries or where they are situated in this country.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
There is only one small point which I would like to raise which has been raised by other members of this group in previous years, particularly the hon. member for Kindersley. This concerns the standardization of weights and measures and sizes of products manufactured in Canada.
I am quite sure that every hon. member has gone downtown and has purchased or has intended to purchase a pair of shoes or a shirt or particularly children's clothing. When they walk into a store they expect that if they buy a child's shirt size six it is going to fit a child aged six but when they get it home it will fit a child three years of age or a child of eight or nine. This has, for a number of years, caused a good deal of concern to every housewife and, I am quite sure, to other people. When you enter a store to buy a pair of shoes, for example, and you recall that the last time you bought a pair of size nine it was a good fit, you expect that that size will still fit. If it does not, it does not necessarily mean that your feet have grown bigger, it simply means that the manufacturer did not use a standard measurement for his product. This has been a big problem in respect to our trade, particularly in connection with items of wearing apparel, and also in relation to imported goods. I am quite sure that the people of Canada would appreciate something being done to standardize many commodities.
There is another aspect of standardization to which I would like to draw the attention
Supply-Trade and Commerce of the minister and that is with respect to Canadian produced goods. Shirts, for instance, are sometimes labelled 100 per cent wool while in many cases they are made of fabricated material and have no connection with sheep. Similarly, when a product is labelled washable or unshrinkable the Canadian people, in my opinion, have the right to assume that that product will meet with the standards implied by its label. We all know that this is not always so.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, before I proceed to make any formal comments about the general question of trade, I should like to express my thanks to the hon. member for Vancouver South for the rather timid endorsation he made of C.C.F. policy a while ago, and also express my appreciation for the few statistics he placed on the record regarding the total amount of trade with China in terms of dollars. It is most unfortunate, however, that he used only figures relating to the last few years for if he had gone back farther than just a few years we would have had a much clearer picture of the trading relationship between Canada and China in terms of dollar value.
One important statement the hon. gentleman made which I believe requires a great deal of amplification or explanation was to the effect that we cannot now recognize in a diplomatic way the government of red China. Hon. members will recall that I asked him if he would care to elaborate on why we cannot and he declined my invitation. If there was any reason behind his making the definite statement that we cannot now undertake to recognize China in a formal and diplomatic fashion I would appreciate it very much if at some future time in this particular vote the minister would undertake to explain whether or not the attitude expressed by the hon. member for Vancouver South represents the policy of the government, and I make that request being fully cognizant of the fact that this is not a debate on external affairs nor a discussion of the estimates of that department.
If it is the policy of the government that we cannot recognize China diplomatically I believe this country is entitled to a clear explanation of this position. Although this is not the time for a discussion on external affairs, as I have said, I think we should be allowed a bit of leeway in discussing the question of the diplomatic recognition of a
2344	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce country because it has a direct bearing on our trade relationship with the countries of the world and in this case with China. I hope, Mr. Chairman, you will allow us to pursue the question of diplomatic recognition to the extent of permitting the minister to explain the position of the government and the reason for its taking that position with respect to expanded trade with red China.
The general tenor of the minister's opening remarks was that Canada is a trading nation and depends on export markets for a great deal of its economic stability-or instability, whichever it happens to be at a given moment-and I believe he said that one out of five persons employed in Canada was employed because of export trade, or if you prefer having it expressed in this fashion, 20 per cent of our economy is dependent upon our export markets.
I intend to confine my remarks on this vote to the attitude of the government-as hon. members may have expected-as it relates to our trading relations with red China. I do so for a number of reasons, probably the most important of which is that China embraces 25 or 30 per cent of the world's population and if the birth rate continues at its present level it will constitute an even greater percentage of the world's population in years to come.
Another important reason for confining my remarks to our relationship with red China is that coming from British Columbia and having some familiarity with the lumber industry-having worked in and around it for eight or ten years-it naturally has a strong personal appeal for me. Lumber, as many hon. gentlemen know, accounts for 35 to 40 per cent of the total economy of the province of British Columbia. That percentage is an indefinite figure. I do not know if anybody can come up with an absolute figure to represent the percentage of the economy of British Columbia that is dependent on the lumber industry because of its extensive ramifications but I believe that 35 to 40 per cent is a generally accepted estimate of the relationship of the lumber industry to the balance of the economy of the province of British Columbia.
One of the best known persons in the lumber industry in British Columbia is Mr. H. R. MacMillan who was head of MacMillan and Bloedel a lumber firm which is one of the largest integrated lumber concerns in the world, I believe second only to the Weyerhauser interests in the United States. For a number of years we in the C.C.F. have been insisting upon formal recognition being given by Canada of the Peoples' Republic of China and secondly upon the expansion of our trade with that country. We


were ridiculed on many occasions for having taken that stand. We were accused of being fellow travellers and merely wanting to support the communist ideology which is an accusation, I think, very few people would make today. Nevertheless that was the accusation that was made against us some years ago.
Mr. MacMillan would not, I think, be one who would have such an accusation directed against him. He made a visit to China not too long ago and upon his return one of his statements was that China is in need of lumber, that we can sell lumber to China and that we should expand our trade to China in terms of lumber. By confining my remarks in this context to lumber I do not want it to be construed that I am implying that wheat and other commodities should not be sold to that country or that the same amount of effort should not be put into selling other products there.
Reference has been made to Mr. Muir, president of the Royal Bank of Canada, who recently returned from a tour of China. His remarks and opinions have become well known throughout the nation and have been mentioned in this house on a number of occasions. I do not believe it is necessary for me to reiterate them or point out the great emphasis he placed on the necessity of expanding trade with that country and I shall refrain from doing so with the exception of re-emphasizing Mr. Muir's comments to the effect that it was galling to see other western nations drumming up business in China while we sat back and were not participating in this. It is significant to note that Mr. Muir made no mention of who these other western nations were but I think we can take it that one of them naturally would be the United Kingdom who extended the diplomatic courtesy to China some years ago and as a result of that has been increasing its total amount of trade with that country almost ever since it first extended diplomatic recognition. These figures were put on the record today by my friend from Vancouver South. I wish that he had undertaken to make some reference to the dollar trade that existed between Canada and China prior to the war.
An article in Canadian Business of October, 1957, plumped for two things: one, extended trade; and, two, the question of diplomatic recognition. It pointed out that prior to the war Canada's trade with China, only as it related to lumber and lumber products, averaged $29 million a year. That was the average of our exports to China prior to the war compared with a figure of $1,700,000 for the total of all products, most of which I understand was ammonium sulphate. This

figure was mentioned this afternoon. It gives some indication to the committee of the great need which exists in China for lumber. I should like to refer to some figures which I have prepared and some figures which have been quoted. China's minister of forestry, whose name is Liang Hsi, commented upon China's needs for timber. This is the statement:
By the end of the second five-year plan China will need 47 million cubic metres of timber a year.
To convert cubic metres into understandable terms so far as we apply them in British Columbia or in Canada, and thinking in terms of a thousand feet board measure, we can use two methods to turn the 47 million cubic metres into Canadian measurement units. It depends on whether he was talking about ordinary log measurement or about processed, finished lumber measurement. If he was referring to the requirement of 47 million cubic metres in terms of whole log measurements and if we convert that to board feet we find that their annual requirements would be 10,340 million board feet per year; that is, in whole log requirements. Incidentally, that is twice as much as the total average annual cut for the entire province of British Columbia in any one year over the past four or five years. If he was talking in terms of finished lumber, then we have to use another conversion factor and we come up with approximately 19J billion board feet requirement a year for China. In China they have a bit more accessible forest acreage than we have in British Columbia but they certainly have far less than Canada has in terms of accessible forest acreage, and their total production is far less also, even if they were fully exploiting their timber resources, which they are not, they would not come anywhere near filling the requirements of that nation.
Quite frankly, Mr. Chairman, the minister is still missing the boat in promoting the sale of goods-not only lumber but other goods as well-to China. I merely mention lumber because of its proximity and its value to the province from which I come.
