Mr. Chairman, I should like to join with the other members who have congratulated the Minister of Trade and Commerce on giving us a long awaited statement on the trade policy of the government. I want to go even a little farther and thank him for his assurance that the present policy of the government is to expand trade with all parts of the world in contrast to the diversionist policy about which we heard so much in the past two elections. If there is one tenet of political faith that has distinguished the Liberal party from all other


political parties it certainly has been our stand on world trade. The Liberal party has always stood for the expansion of world trade in all directions and to all parts of the world so as to build up as far as possible a great world trading community. The statement of the minister this afternoon in which he gave us the assurance that this was now the policy of the government has gladdened not only the hearts of my colleagues on this side of the house but I am sure of all the people of Canada.
The minister emphasized quite rightly the importance of trade in the economy of our country and its impact on the employment situation. If trade is important to Canada as a whole it is doubly so to the maritime provinces which had to sacrifice their trading position in the markets of the world in order to make Canada a nation. What is true of the maritime provinces is even more true of the province of Newfoundland which since 1949 has become a captive market.
Prior to 1949 we were able to trade in the world markets and take advantage of the best bargains that we could obtain but since 1949 we have been compelled to make the bulk of our purchases from mainland Canada. If the trade of Newfoundland were to be compared with our trade with foreign countries I think it would be shown that Newfoundland would be the equivalent of Canada's second or third best trading customer because the value of our trade as a province with mainland Canada must run somewhere around $200 million or more a year.
In Newfoundland we have some small industries we are trying to develop and which, as in other parts of Canada, we must develop if we are going to provide jobs for the increase in our population. But the development of those industries depends almost entirely upon our ability to sell our products either on the mainland or in world markets. In that respect we are very greatly handicapped because of our geographical position and the terrific transportation costs which are a greater handicap to us than to any other part of Canada. At other times in the house I have stressed the importance of helping these local industries where possible by making defence purchases locally and by granting them defence contracts in products which we are able to supply.
I have pointed out on earlier occasions how we are not able to compete on tenders because our transportation costs more than offset our lower factory prices. I brought up this matter in the defence committee and asked if some special preference could not be given to local industries in the maritimes and Newfoundland. I was told that if this were done it

would be as much a handicap as an advantage. I then discussed the problem with Mr. Donald Gordon in the railway committee and he pointed out that his hands were tied by certain laws which prevented him from discriminating between one part of Canada and another. Whatever rate he made for Newfoundland would have to apply to the same commodity everywhere in Canada.
We seem to be getting up a blind alley but nevertheless there is a definite need for some form of preference if our local industries are to thrive and develop. I know that the minister is a very ingenious person.
I hope he will bring his ingenuity to bear on the problem and try to find some way of according preferential treatment to our small local industries in the maritime provinces and Newfoundland.
Since nearly all my constituents are fishermen, Mr. Chairman, like my colleague, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, I shall confine my remarks mainly to the marketing of fish. Last year Canada produced 1.9 billion pounds of fish. I should like to emphasize that that figure is the landed weight because obviously the processed weight would be very different. That figure was slightly lower than the 2 billion pounds landed weight for the previous year. This volume of fish had a landed value of $93 million. I should like to draw hon. members' attention to the fact that this is the landed value as compared with the $132.5 million which the minister mentioned in his speech this afternoon which, of course, would be the market value of that fish.
Now, of that 1.9 billion pounds of fish landed, 548 million pounds or 28 per cent represented the production of Newfoundland and had a landed value of around $13 million or roughly 14 per cent of the total value. When we compare these figures, even when allowance is made for the different market values of the different species, I think the figures prove that the Newfoundland fisherman is still getting far less than the average landed value of the product he produces.
Of that 548 million pounds, 52.6 million pounds were processed and sold as frozen fillets. This figure represents a decline of 16 per cent from the 62.8 million pounds of frozen fillets which were produced in the previous year. All of these 52.6 million pounds of fish were sold in the United States market. Hon. members will, therefore, appreciate our delight at the minister's statement this afternoon when he stressed that trade relations with the United States were of paramount importance. If they are of paramount importance to the whole of Canada, then that statement is doubly true in so far as Newfoundland is concerned. Any worsening of
Supply-Trade and Commerce these trade relations which would motivate reprisals in the United States market, such as the establishment of quotas or setting up tariffs against our fish, would be a tragedy to the fishermen of Newfoundland.
The remainder of that fish was processed with salt and sold in the salt fish markets of the world, either as dried salted fish, wet salted fish or pickled fish. About 100 years ago Newfoundland produced 1.5 million quintals of dried fish. For the benefit of hon. members who might not be familiar with this term, I should explain that a quintal is a hundredweight, 112 pounds of dried fish. From 1930 to 1949 our production of dried salted fish hovered around the one million quintal mark. Some years it went a little above, and some years slightly below. If one averaged it, it would average out at a little more than one million quintals a year.
Since confederation in 1949 that figure has steadily declined until today our production of salt fish is a little over 600,000 quintals, which represents a reduction of about 40 per cent. This reduction has taken place in the face of an increase in world production, and an increase in world consumption of salted fish. The decline has been caused by two factors. One factor was the Marshall plan which came into effect after the war and enabled our customers in the European markets to build modern fishing boats and to produce part of their own consumption. Part of the decline was the result of the impact of confederation on our trading position. Prior to confederation Newfoundland enjoyed the advantage of the best of two possible worlds. We had a dollar currency of our own, we had a surplus of dollars and we had a sterling deficit. Consequently it was possible for us to sell our fish in the sterling markets, use the proceeds to reduce our sterling debt and take the equivalent of that out of our surplus dollars to pay the fishermen.
The marketing machinery which the government had set up made it possible for the fishermen to know exactly how much they were going to get for their catch before they even produced it. After confederation that set of conditions was changed entirely. As a result our salt fish market has steadily worsened, and the position of our fishermen of being able to tell just what the prospects of the fishing industry might be has steadily deteriorated. When we produced a million and a half quintals of dried fish we were able to sell half a million quintals of dried salted fish in the Brazilian market. Last year we sold 27,560 quintals in that market. If we go back to 1953 we see that the market has fluctuated from 17,000 quintals in 1953 to 59,000 in 1954; down to 681 quintals in 1955; down even lower to 446 quintals in 1956 and

Supply-Trade and Commerce up to 27,500 quintals last year. That is a long way from the large market that we used to enjoy in Brazil. We know, as the minister pointed out today, that a large part of this decline was caused by the currency problem from which Brazil is suffering now. But surely, it should be possible for us to do something to help Brazil purchase more of this fish because it is an old and established market. What are your suggestions?
Has the government no policy?
You make me Minister of Trade and Commerce and I will give you plenty of suggestions.
The hon. member is doing very well now.

The Mediterranean market which used to be one of our greatest markets has now dwindled because of the factors which I mentioned a few minutes ago down to about 15 per cent of our catch. Last year we marketed only 120,000 quintals in the whole Mediterrannean area. Of that amount 7J per cent or 50,000 quintals went to Italy. That is not right.
Those are the figures.
Those figures are not right.

The minister can give the correct figures. What we sold to the Portuguese in the last two years is negligible
[Mr. Carter.)

and that in spite of the fact that Portugal would not be able to compete with Newfoundland if we did not provide them with harbour facilities, bait facilities and many other advantages which we give to them. I think we have a bargaining point that we could use with Portugal to better advantage than we are doing at the present time. Thirty-three per cent of our fish was sold in North America, and most of that went to mainland buyers who bought the fish wet salted or in salt bulk condition, reprocessed it and resold it again mainly to the Cuban market.
But here in Canada we have another opportunity of expanding our market for fish. I should like to see a great joint advertising program conducted by the government and the fish trades-possibly the provincial government may come in also but certainly the industry and the federal government- directed towards making this product better known across Canada. Salted fish can be a great delicacy if it is properly cooked. However, I will say that very few Canadians know how to cook it. Nevertheless there are people who are specialists. You can find them in Brazil and in Portugal. I think it would be worth while to bring a few of them over here and to have them travel around Canada cooking a bit of salted fish for our Canadian brothers and getting them to develop a taste for this delicacy.
Where is your apron?

I am not a cook, I am a connoisseur. I think that winds up what I wanted to say about salted fish, Mr. Chairman, but there is much more that could be said because there are many factors to be taken into consideration when one comes to discuss the trading policy of a country like Canada. I refer to such factors as exchange rates and problems in connection with conversion of currency. I might say that the premium on the Canadian dollar at this present time is an additional hardship for the fresh fish processors who are obliged to sell their fish wholly in the United States market. There is the problem of stability of currency, of transportation costs to which I have referred and subsidies, indirect and direct, which my friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate dealt with this afternoon.
Before I sit down I should like to say one word about trade with China. I do not know whether or not we should trade with China and I do not think any one here tonight has enough wisdom to know whether or not we should do so. Certainly if there is one point on which we need divine guidance, this is it. A very good case can be made out for trading with China and a very good case can be

made out for not trading with China. As Macaulay once said, I wish I could be as cocksure about one thing as my hon. friends to my right are about everything.
When we come to consider a matter of this kind I think it really boils down to a question of motive: Why do we want to do it? The rightness or the wrongness or the ultimate good cannot be divorced from our motives, no matter what our action is. I know we have a very popular doctrine which is called enlightened self-interest; and selfinterest, as it implies, is based on some selfish purpose, some selfish benefit. If it is selfish, if an action is based solely on something that we are going to get out of it for ourselves, then in the long run it is not in our best interests; and if it is not in our best interests, it is not enlightened. Hence enlightened self-interest is, in my opinion, a term that is contradictory. But whether we do so or whether we do not, I should like to point out this fact. Our friends the red Chinese and our friends the Russians do not act on the motive of self-interest. They are not one bit concerned whether it is going to increase the prosperity of their country, increase their volume of trade, reduce a surplus or anything else. That matter does not count at all with them. Only one thing counts and it is this: Will it further their objective of winning the cold war? Will it further their goals of spreading their philosophy all over the world and enslaving the peoples of the world? We should be equally anxious not only to frustrate that objective but to see to it that we on our part are motivated in the direction that is going to support the way of life to which we all subscribe.

First of all, Mr. Chairman, I should like to congratulate the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the government generally for their efforts to correct this tendency with regard to trade which has reached such great proportions in recent years as to cause the Canadian people in the space of approximately ten months twice to endorse the policy of this government and to turn a house of about 170 Liberals into a house of approximately 200 Conservative members. This political upheaval in the history of our country is significant, particularly when you consult the record in respect of trade in agricultural products.
Something has been said in this house during this debate about wheat marketings and the wheat marketing policies of this government. I think the hon. member for Ottawa West tried to a certain extent to take some of the credit away from this government for the magnificent job it has done in increasing marketings of grain from this
Supply-Trade and Commerce country in world markets. I would like to say a few things in that regard. One thing this government did was to appoint a wheat committee to study this situation and endeavour to take those steps necessary to increase the marketing of grain in the world markets.
During the election campaign I had the pleasure of a visit to my constituency by no less a person than the Leader of the Opposition in this House of Commons. In speaking in one of the towns there he dealt with the problems of trade and agriculture. Among the things he said, as outlined in a press report given wide distribution, was the following:
I want to mention, finally, one other specific measure that would be of direct and immediate benefit to farmers in western Canada. Liberal governments in the past did their best to ensure the maximum possible sales of Canadian grain, but large surpluses accumulated despite all our efforts -and nobody has been able to show that his efforts would be, or are, any better than ours were,
In this connection I would point out that in 1956-57, 260 million bushels of wheat were marketed and in 1957-58-that is to say, to July 9-296.7 million bushels of wheat were marketed and there still remain 21 days of the marketing season to be taken into account. When he was in my constituency the Leader of the Opposition had other things to say on this subject and I would like to give a further quotation as follows:
In terms of over-all measures which will aid farmers, next to maintaining a strong domestic economy, is an aggressive sales policy for wheat. While there has been much difficulty in maintaining and increasing farm exports, we assert that Liberal policies of reciprocal removal of trade barriers and of international co-operation hold the greatest promise-and are indispensable in expanding export markets for wheat, other grains, for apples and potatoes, and for livestock products. Because of the present and potential opportunity of our farmers in the great American market, we would propose to encourage and develop that market- and not destroy it by hostility to the United States. Every livestock producer in Canada knows what damage can be done to his sales and prices if he is cut off from the American market and that danger is increased by some of the policies of the present government-
All I can say in that regard is that when this government took office, the sales of livestock to the American market were practically nil. The fact is, if you take a close look at the statistics you cannot help but realize that about the only kind of cattle going into the United States market were purebred cattle at that time, and in regard to his allegation that we were stirring up hostilities I would like to point out that sales to the great United States market have reached proportions unmatched and at prices unmatched in many years.

The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo also had something to say in regard to trade, particularly with respect to China. He did not know whether we should trade with China or not, but his leader knew what he wanted to do. During the election campaign at Cud worth he had this to say:
We should also press hard to develop more markets-in Asia for instance-including China.
The interesting thing about that, so far as I am concerned, is that I believe he thought we could not sell wheat to China, but hardly had he left the hall before it was announced that wheat sales were being effected to China.
There are a number of things which could be said in this regard but all I wish to say at this time is that with respect to free trade, and I believe every member in this house believes in free trade although the Liberal party thinks that they are the only ones who do. The Liberal party was in power for 22 years and we must remember that when they left office the Canadian government was receiving more revenue from tariffs through the treasury of this country than at any time in this history.
That is true.

Because of the volume of
our trade.

This is something we
should consider. If I have a cow for sale and you want to buy that cow, free trade ends right there. This is because I am going to try to get as much for that cow as I can and you are going to try to pay as little for it as you can. Among the remarks made this afternoon was one to the effect that the Liberal party is a party which will work with all nations in respect of their trade programs. rather a bad position with many of those other countries.
I will conclude my remarks at this time although many other things will come up during the estimates on which I may wish to say a word or two. Mr. Chairman, I readily
agreed with the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he said this afternoon that international trade was of vital importance to the Canadian economy and it is because I feel this is so and because I feel that the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce are also so important that I believe it is all the more regrettable that the leader of the house and the government did not deem it necessary to give the house adequate advance notice of the fact that these estimates were to be brought forward today. This practice of not giving sufficient notice is becoming more and more frequent and I think it is an unfair practice. As a matter of fact we might consider it as a sneaky form of closure.
Oh, oh.

International trade, of course, has played in the past and is now playing an extremely important part in our economy. And because, of course, Canada will always have a greater capacity for production than for absorption we can expect that exports of Canadian products will continue to play an increasingly important role in our economy in the future. The maintenance and increase of our international trade will not be any easier for this government than it was for the previous government.
The field of international trade is now occupied by all the nations of the world who feel more keenly than at any other time in their history the importance and the necessity of international trade, and because of the differences in the standard of living of the different countries of the world and because

of the low costs of production and transportation of, I would say, the majority of our competitors, markets willing to pay Canadian prices for Canadian products will be more and more diificult to find in the future.
There is a factor, of course, that will also make our trade more difficult in the future and that is that in the evolution of trade we have seen the creation of economic blocs such as the European customs union and the proposed European free trade area. I believe we can expect to see more of these economic blocs in the future in different areas of the world and I do not doubt that a day may come when Canada will have to be part of one of these blocs.
The fourth reason why international trade for Canada may be more and more difficult is the fact that the U.S.S.R. and the satellites have now engaged in an economic war against the western world. There is no doubt in my mind that in the military field the western world is really capable of defending itself. There is a question in my mind, though, of the ability of the western world to defend itself in the economic field. I sincerely hope we do have all the requisites to adequately defend ourselves in the economic war that Russia is now waging and as a result of which Canada may find it still more difficult to find an increasingly prosperous share of the international trade field.
There is no question of the importance of international trade for Canada nor is there, I believe, any difference of opinion about the difficulty that exists in our being able to achieve for Canada this increasingly important economic factor. We were all very interested to hear the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce this afternoon. We all listened very attentively but I am afraid it was impossible to detect in the words the minister spoke any indication of what the government's trade policy might conceivably be. Listening to the minister one gets the impression that the Conservatives still labour under the illusion that they can talk their way into the markets of the commonwealth, of Europe and of the world. The Conservatives have indeed done a lot of talking and have succeeded in confusing every one concerned. They have also contradicted by their actions all the talk in which they had previously engaged.
For example, in the short space of one year we saw the government enter into a 15 per cent diversion policy under which 15 per cent of Canada's trade was going to be diverted from the United States to the United Kingdom and that, of course, certainly did not please the people of the United States. Later during that year the government decided to send a trade mission to Europe and
Supply-Trade and Commerce there the government of Canada assured the British traders that it would indeed buy a great deal more from Britain than from the United States. Finally, just a short time ago, the government decided to raise the British preferential tariff on wool and that, of course, did not please the British traders. Indeed, it confused them and caused them a good deal of concern. In the brief period of one year it would appear that the government has succeeded in antagonizing its two very best customers. That, as a policy of international trade, could not possibly be worse.
The Conservatives have frequently accused the Liberals of having lost Canada's markets overseas. Many speeches were made by hon. gentlemen opposite on that subject but not once did any speaker say what markets in Europe were lost, how they were lost or why they were lost. It is only when we read the budget speech that we begin to realize that the Conservatives have begun to appreciate some of the problems affecting our overseas markets. In his budget speech, as recorded at page 1250 of Hansard of June 17, 1958, the Minister of Finance is reported as saying:
Moreover, I confess my concern over costs of production and prices in Canada. Only by keeping our costs of production in line with those of our competitors can we hope to achieve expanding employment and progressive improvement in our standard of living.
We are in danger of becoming a high-cost economy. Such a prospect is particularly perilous in the case of a country like Canada which must sell so much of its production in markets abroad. Moreover, Canadian producers are encountering increasing difficulty in retaining their domestic market in the face of keen competition from abroad. Many of them under these circumstances turn to the government for a solution of their cost problem.
One would get the impression that the minister has come to the conclusion that these problems suddenly arose since the time the Conservative government came to power. That is, of course, not true. This high-cost economy has existed in our country since world war II. It is one of the reasons why markets may have been lost in that period just as in this period under the present government they are still continuing to be lost.
However at no time during the Liberal regime did the Liberals either by their policies, their words or their actions ever jeopardize foreign markets let alone the markets of our two very best customers as the Prime Minister did by engaging in the 15 per cent trade diversion in his never-ending quest for sensational legislation.
I think it is ridiculous, if it were not so pathetic, to hear the Prime Minister trying now to deny his trade diversion policy of a year ago. This afternoon in his speech, the Minister of Trade and Commerce also appeared to be seeking to deny it when he

Of course, the government has tried to justify this 15 per cent diversion policy because of the very unfortunate and formidable trade deficit between Canada and the United States. Neither the previous government nor any Canadian was indifferent to the Canadian trade deficit with the United States. It was certainly not considered by anyone on this side of the house to be an ideal situation at any time, but it seems to me that the whole foreign trade problem was at that time and still is so vital to our Canadian economy that it would have been foolish indeed, as it has been proven to be, to try to change a natural trade pattern which the prevailing world trends, competition, prices and standards of living have now forced on our economy.
I respectfully submit that this increased competition in world markets today is a sufficient challenge to our economy without having the government embark on a half-baked, half-thought-out policy of repudiating existing markets no matter where those markets may be.
There is nothing more half-baked than that.

Perhaps not. It is very difficult indeed to understand the logic or the lack of logic behind the government's action on

the question of trade, but it is absolutely impossible to find any definite government trade policy. It is also difficult, Mr. Chairman, to understand the attitude of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I really do not know of anyone whose personality has changed so rapidly in the short space of one year. From a very genial, very loquacious, very affable member, he has indeed, I am afraid, turned into a more or less taciturn and even at times a cynical member of this house. One has only to read or, better still, to listen to the Minister of Trade and Commerce answering questions on trade to get the impression that the minister greatly resents being queried as to what is actually going on in his own particular ivory tower.
I had the temerity to ask the minister a question on trade and I as the rest of my colleagues, also received the minister's usual supercilious and evasively empty answers. On June 11, as reported at page 1033 of Hansard, I reworded a question that I had asked the minister previously. The question read:
1.	What was the total amount of Canadian dollars paid to the United States in 1956 for imports of farm tractors manufactured in the United Kingdom and assembled in the United States?
2.	Was this amount taken into consideration by the dominion bureau of statistics when compiling its figures regarding the Canadian trade deficit with the United States?
3.	Are other products manufactured in the United Kingdom and imported into Canada from the United States? If so, what items?
4.	Has the government taken any steps to encourage British companies to assemble farm tractors and other British products in Canada rather than in the United States? If so, with what results?
I received the following answer, as recorded at page 1034 of Hansard:

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
This question, Mr. Speaker, is a refurbished edition of the one asked by the hon. gentleman last session on January 29, 1958. My answer on that occasion will be the one I give now. It is as follows:
"Mr. Speaker, no records such as are asked for by the hon. member are kept, and the information is not easily obtainable as it involves tracing the country of origin of components in manufactured articles coming from the United States."
I can hardly conceive the very brilliant, very efficient and alert Minister of Trade and Commerce not being aware of an article that appeared in the Gazette concerning the trade mission in Britain about which we have heard unfortunately far too little since its return to this country. I am quite sure this article had been given to the minister by the very efficient officers of his department and I cannot understand why the minister was so evasive. I should like to quote the article that appeared in the Montreal Gazette of November 29, 1957:
Coventry, England, November 28-(CP)-Members of Canada's trade mission learned with surprise

today that Britain's trade deficit with Canada is not as large as officially reported.
Officials of the Massey-Harris-Ferguson tractor firm said that a large portion of the $150 million Canadians spent last year for so-called United States tractors and parts actually flowed back to Britain.
Many of the component parts of the Massey-Harris tractors sold in Canada were assembled at Detroit but produced in the big Standard Motor Car Company in Coventry.
William Perlin of St. John's, Newfoundland, a mission member, observed that if this is the case the mission has been labouring under a misconception. The Canadian bureau of statistics had reported that last year, for example Britain had a deficit of some $330 million in Canadian trade. Canada was reported to have a deficit in United States trade of some $1,300 million.
If a proportion of the money Canadians have spent on Massey-Harris tractors imported from the United States actually came back to Britain, then it apeared that Britain's deficit with Canada and Canada's deficit with the United States were not as large as were reported.
James Patterson of Winnipeg, president of the interprovincial farm union council, said he would like to see steps taken to have the Canadian statistics corrected.
The 50-man mission was split up to visit the various motor car companies in this area. Some went to Standard, others to the Rolls-Royce, Jaguar, Rootes and Rover plants.
Ian Wallace, a director of Massey-Harris-Ferguson, joined Alick S. Dick, managing director of Standard, to show some of the members the motor car and tractor production there. Standard produces the Massey-Harris tractor under contract in what was described as the biggest tractor plant in the world.
Wallace explained that the reason why Britain ships tractors to Canada by way of the United States is because Americans are not fond of buying foreign-made goods. If the tractors, for example, were assembled in Canada and sold in the United States, there might be some American sales resistance.
On the other hand, Canada allows tractors in duty free. Tractors could be assembled conveniently in the United States to supply both the Canadian and American market. The parent company of Massey-Harris-Ferguson is in Canada. Subsidiaries are located in the United States, Britain and other countries.
Dick, whose company produces the Vanguard and Triumph motor vehicles, said vehicle production runs about 350 units a day. Tractor production, running at 380 units daily, now is being boosted to 415 with expansion concentrated on a new model of some 50 horsepower. The well-laid-out $50 million plant employs 10,500 workers.
At a luncheon of lobster, steak and wine, Dick urged Canadians to buy more Massey-Harris tractors "for the good of British trade".
Well, Mr. Chairman, that is one for the book. British industrialists are encouraging members of the Canadian trade commission in Britain to buy more tractors from the United States for the good of British trade. I am beginning to see why the Prime Minister is backing away from his 15 per cent trade diversion and why his Minister of Trade and Commerce is now feeling that trade with the United States is of paramount importance. I must say that we on this side of the house have certainly no objection in
Supply-Trade and Commerce helping British trade and in trying to promote more British trade. But I also feel that if we are going to do that the British would also be willing to help us when we are in a very difficult economic situation.
There are two items at least in this article which I think should be noted. First of all, the trade deficit between the United Kingdom and Canada and between Canada and the United States was less by at least $150 million for 1956 and, of course, there may be other items imported from the United States which are manufactured in Great Britain. I understand the minister's point of view when he says it is difficult to obtain information as to the origin of some of the machinery or parts of machinery that are brought in from the United States but surely it would be in keeping with the tradition of the dominion bureau of statistics not to allow a $150 million error to slip into its figures as to the real trade deficit.
Like Mr. James Patterson of Winnipeg, the president of the interprovincial farm union council, I too should like to see steps taken in order that the dominion bureau of statistics figures may be changed with respect to this matter. I also think it might be well worth while, if at all possible, to check to see just how much material coming into Canada from the United States is being manufactured in Great Britain.
There is another point I should like to make. A while ago I said I felt sure that Great Britain would be willing to help us while we were in a difficult economic situation because of the good will we show Great Britain and, of course, to me, aid is always a two-way affair. It is mutual. I see no reason why the $150 million worth of tractors bought for Canadian consumption in 1956 from the United States could not have been assembled in Canadian plants where there is far more unemployment at the present time than is usual at this time of year. I do not see why this could not be done now. I feel that by doing so we would still be helping Great Britain. The money would go directly to Great Britain but we would be employing our own people. If the minister is embarrassed about trying to find a suitable plant for the assembling of such tractors, may I remind him that in my own town we have Sorel Industries where if no work is given to the company within a relatively short time it will have to close its doors and let out a substantial number of employees.
Before taking my seat may I say that I should very much like the minister to give the house a clear briefing on the results achieved by the trade mission to England. I agree with the minister that international
2354	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce trade is of the utmost importance to Canada, and if we are to take our part in the very difficult international picture it is equally important that the government should have a very definite trade policy, particularly if the government does not want to repeat at the trade conference to be held in September the fiasco of the last trade conference.

Mr. Chairman, I have a number of questions I want to put to the minister that could be answered later when we get into the details of the estimates but because of their general nature I think it might be fairer to ask them now. The first one could be answered tonight. A few weeks ago a magnificent criticism was presented in the house of the fair at Brussels and the Canadian exhibit and I wondered whether the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska had been dispatched to Brussels again to improve the whole tone of the Canadian part in the exhibition.
One of the questions I want to ask reaches ahead to 1961 and the next census. As the minister is aware, I am interested in the problem of redistribution. The census will be taken in 1961 and I understand that normally the results as to population for use in redistribution are available in March of the following year. With its experience in the census of 1956 I should like to know whether the bureau of statistics will be in a position to give us an answer more quickly this time so far as these figures are concerned because I think it might be quite important if the political situation is projected four years ahead. If we do not get these results in March and if redistribution is to be carried out by parliament it could be very rushed should the Prime Minister in his wisdom decide to have a summer election. By pushing the thing ahead six weeks or two months we could conceivably save ourselves from fighting the 1962 or 1963 election on the basis of the 1951 census. I suggest to the minister and to other members of the house that that would be very unfair to a great many voters of the country although it might also, if there are changes, be a little unfair to some of the present members.
Would you like another March election?

I think March is a splendid time to have an election-the ides of March. I also wanted to ask the minister for a bit more detail on the small business set-up foreshadowed supposedly by the appointment of the new associate deputy minister of trade. Perhaps at some point later in the discussion of the estimates the minister might be able


to spell out for us a bit more of the framework of that organization and what its scope is going to be.

I wonder whether I might reply to that immediately. No decision has been reached yet as to which department will have the responsibility for the proposed small business section. It may be the Department of Trade and Commerce but it is a bit premature to discuss the matter at the moment because a decision has not yet been reached.

It would seem to appear then that my question was very hypothetical, as must have been much of the press speculation on this matter. Another question which I think the minister could deal with more fully before we leave this part of his estimates is the campaign that such distinguished gentlemen as Stuart Armour are trying to get under way to buy Canadian. I think we should have a fuller explanation of the part the minister's department might play in that regard and, if we are going to go out to persuade people to buy Canadian, especially what ramifications that may have upon our external trade policies. I think the "buy Canadian" theme is something that our people should literally buy at the present time.
In the remarks of opposition members so far in the debate today it has been noticeable that there has been quite a bit of jollying the government with respect to its reaction to the Thorneycroft proposals and even more jollying on its reneging as to the absolute clearness of the 15 per cent trade diversion suggestion. From what I have read and have been able to learn about the matter I actually think the government was quite smart to give the Thorneycroft proposals the brush-off and I also think they were very clever in going slow on the 15 per cent diversion plan.
I wonder whether or not the minister is conversant at all with a report that has been put out in the United States by the Rockefeller Brothers fund, entitled "Economic Policy for the Twentieth Century". This particular report has received a great deal of analysis in the United States periodical press, much of it favourable. The report, of course, concentrates upon the communist threat to free world trade.
One of the suggestions made in the report is that we build up regional groups of trading nations. One gathers from the reactions to the report one finds in the Congressional Record that it has been favourably received. Another suggestion is to establish an interAmerican trade authority. The report contains some reference to Canada, and says: The United States should participate in calling as soon as possible an inter-American economic conference in which Canada would be invited.

The conference should be called for the joint consideration of an action to-
Find workable procedures for moderating extreme price fluctuations in commodity trades.
Devise ways for the co-operative promotion of general economic growth and development, including consideration of an inter-American development authority.
Work toward international agreement to set up a common market of hemisphere wide scope or of regional common markets with merger as an eventual goal.
Of course, we would have to understand that any idea of merger would be a long-range development.
Establish an inter-American payments union to provide for the full convertibility of currencies among all nations subscribing to a common market arrangement.
Facilitate other inter-American arrangements for co-operation upon common purposes and social objectives in such fields as education, low-cost housing, health and technical assistance.
Assure that such arrangements shall be so conceived and executed as to promote high levels of multilateral world trade and the general economic growth of the entire free world.
The idea of a number of regional trading groups in the free world it seems to me, so far as Canada is concerned, is quite as sensible as Canada trying to place itself within a commonwealth trade group. It almost seems to me that we are allowing sentiment and patriotism, of the kind that I am sure most of us feel, to confuse what are our real interests so far as trade is concerned. While the government and all the rest of us are associated with, and stuck with the problems of United States investment in our economy, I do not think we can shy away from the fact that it is the United States economy, the inter-American economy, within which our destiny largely lies. This suggestion put forward in the Rockefeller Brothers fund report seems to me to be a good one. I should like to see the minister take some action to follow it up after what I am sure will be a dearth of results from the commonwealth conference that we are having later this year. I would suggest to him that, now that the election is out of the way and we do not have to worry about it for three or four years, we get away from these favourite slogans that pop up in elections and become much more realistic in our attitude towards United States trade.
There is one thing in the Rockefeller report that may give the minister a bit of a lever. It relates to the amount of United States foreign trade and its effect upon the United States economy. I quote:
Within the free-world trading system. United States exports account for 20 per cent of all exports, and its imports for 14 per cent of total imports. But in terms of our domestic economy,
Supply-Trade and Commerce combined imports and exports represent only about eight per cent of annual output. This relatively small proportion often leads us to underestimate the importance of that trade to other nations. What is a small item on our import list may be a major source of revenue for an exporting nation, for example our imports of Swiss watches, Scotch whiskey, or Latin American coffee and copper.
The report goes on to say that between nine and ten per cent of all the durable goods produced in the United States is sold abroad. Significantly enough, these sales provide the margin between profit and loss for a large segment of American industries. About 4,500,000 workers, or seven per cent of the entire United States labour force, are directly dependent upon foreign trade for their livelihoods. Foreign trade provides more direct employment in the United States than the automobile, steel, chemical and textile industries combined.
This picture of the powerful role that that portion of foreign trade plays within the United States economy should give the minister, with his idea of the Canadian nation's trade with the United States, a powerful lever to use in future meetings he might have with United States authorities.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to add a word or two to what has already been said, and deal specifically with the dollar balance of payments between countries in relation to our international trade. If we are to analyse the position of Canada in world markets, and also tackle the job of analysing Canada's foreign trade, we must know something about the dollar exchange balances as they exist between Canada and the countries to whom we wish to sell our products. If we do this, then we have within reach a very good measure of the effective demand of that particular country in relation to the products which we have in Canada and wish to sell.
I say, Mr. Chairman, it is only to the effective demand that we can look at this time in our analysis. In other words, if a country to which we wish to sell products has not the dollar exchange with which to buy our goods, you may have all the demand that you wish in that country but it still will not be effective demand. A proper analysis of foreign trade connotes a study of the dollar exchange balances of the various countries around the world in relation to that of Canada. This enables the demand of a country to be effective. Anything else is non-effective demand. In other words non-effective demand means that the country has not got the dollars with which to buy our products. This further means we either have to lend that country money, give them the goods or take their currency and write off whatever loss that

Supply-Trade and Commerce may entail. It is by means of their dollar exchange balances that they are able to buy, and we must look to their exchange balances to understand if they are in position to buy the goods and services which they desire from us and other countries.
This desire to purchase may cover wheat or other products. Our position, of course, would be to try to sell as much wheat and other Canadian products as possible. But I submit that the Minister of Trade and Commerce no doubt has at his elbow an analysis of the dollar exchange balances between this and other countries. With this information he is in a position to arrive at a close approximation of the trade possibilities of any foreign country.
I do not wish to extend my discussion in this debate except to point out that if we were to come directly to the point and to a discussion of those factors which will add to the exchange balances of those countries and to the expanding of those balances, we would have the most rational approach to an understanding of the present trade position of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I was wondering why the earlier portion of this debate centred so much around fish or the export of fish. I was wondering whether it was not because the government's trade policy or the minister is all at sea fishing for a firm trade policy for Canada. Like all other members of the house, I was most interested in the fine dissertation or thesis presented to the house by the minister which consisted of wishful thinking as to what a trade policy for Canada might be. But for all that wishful thinking in that splendid thesis that he laid down, we did not learn from him precisely what the Canadian trade policy is.
After he had spoken for 30 minutes, and we were certainly expecting some firm statement, we heard nothing from the minister and we allowed him almost 30 minutes additional beyond his regular time hoping and waiting for an announcement from him as to what that trade policy is. As far as we are concerned I have found nothing that could tell me with any degree of precision that: this is our trade policy on this subject or on that subject. We heard a great deal of what we should like to see or what we are hoping it might be but we heard from the minister not a word as to what the policy actually is. I interpret his efforts as that of one genuinely and honestly searching, groping and even stumbling along from one inconsistency in our trade policy to another.


Let us take, for example, the reference that has so frequently been made to the trade mission to the United Kingdom. The minister speaks so ardently, so seriously and so hopefully about our export trade and of the urgency and the importance of increasing it. Yet with great pride he comes into the chamber and presents the story of the United Kingdom trade mission not to increase our export trade but, peculiarly enough, to increase our import trade from Great Britain. We are in favour of it. We support it. But I should have liked to see the reverse also take place, namely a reciprocal arrangement with the United Kingdom that there should be on their part an obligation to take 15 per cent more or at least to increase by 15 per cent their imports into the United Kingdom from Canada.
Then you have the minister's very sanguine hopes and his expression of his dreams about our export trade to Europe. The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres has already quoted the Minister of Finance. The house knows how increasingly difficult our export to Europe is becoming. We certainly cannot burn the candle at both ends.
The Minister of Finance has told us that we are pricing ourselves practically out of the European market. Our cost of production is high. We know that the European cost of production is low. Russian slave labour production, Japanese low-cost labour and other forms of production are now flooding all the markets to which we made appeals during the past number of years. Therefore how can we on the one hand maintain a high-price policy for production in Canada and with that high cost of production expect to get into the markets of Europe where the cost of production is so low? We find there a definite inconsistency.
Then also the Minister of Finance makes an extremely important statement to which I should now like to refer. It is to be found at page 1231 of Hansard of June 17 and is as follows:
Population growth of itself does not ensure progress, but in a country such as ours it has a special significance. It provides a greater market for our agricultural produce and for the products of our factories-
Here we have a situation where the government accepts the fact that if our export markets are dwindling and possibly largely disappearing, the only remedy for our production in Canada is to increase at least our home consumers' market; and with the increase of the home consumers' market certainly we might be able to keep our people more employed. Instead, what do we find?

We find that factories are closing and people are being thrown out of jobs only because of the fact that we have no market for the products we make in Canada. We do not have them abroad and along comes the government with an immigration policy that certainly does not encourage immigration into this country in order to help us to grow and to develop a home consumers' market.
I therefore suggest, Mr. Chairman, that all this groping and uncertainty with regard to a trade policy for Canada is perhaps something that should be expected. The government, perhaps somewhat new in this business, is searching as far as it can but it is focusing most of its attention on its desire to do those things which will enable it to keep election promises. I should like to see the government more courageously take the position of fixing a trade policy irrespective of whether it meets election promises or whether it does not do so. I think the government should take its eye off keeping election promises made last year and this year. I think the government should place the interests of the country far ahead of its interests in hoping to keep election promises which might support its own political party.
I should like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce to quote to the house what new industries have been brought to Canada in the last year or two or what new factories have opened up? I think the minister should concentrate all his attention on the expansion of industry. We have heard, for example, in previous years of new industries. With great pride the minister would report to the house from time to time that a new industry had opened up giving employment to so many people. I have not heard-certainly during the past year-of a single new substantial industry that has opened up in order to expand our production and our work in Canada.
I should like to draw the attention of the minister to the needle trades industry. This industry, which employs perhaps close to 200,000 people across the country, is steadily on the decline. I do not know whether it is the result of tariffs or whether it is the result of other difficulties which exist in the industry. However, one thing is certain. The complaint we hear is that they are having difficulty. There are no new markets.
At one time our country enjoyed a fine export market for clothing, including sports and ladies' clothing, in the British West Indies, but today we do not hear of a dollar's worth of the products of the needle trades being exported to that area. Markets are declining and, what is more, the speed of production is being accelerated so that the
Supply-Trade and Commerce same volume of work is now being produced in half the time. We must build up markets to keep our people at work, but we can readily see that only 50 per cent of the needle trades are required to produce what it took 100 per cent to produce in prior years.
I therefore want to impress upon the minister the fact that the government should present to the house at the first opportunity a courageous trade policy; one that will be consistent and one with which the country can wrestle; something that will enable Canada to go forward, extend its trade and provide employment for our people.
I appeal to the minister especially, following the question raised earlier by the hon. gentlemen who spoke before me, to enlighten this house either during the course of this debate or at a later time with respect to the position of the small businessman. We were hopeful that some relief would be given to small business, but I think we have had a setback in the minister's answer -at least it gave me that impression-when he said that while there may have been some talk about it and while an assistant deputy minister may have been appointed, the government does not yet have a plan ready to be announced. I think the government should at least confirm that the plan previously announced to this house with respect to relief for small tradesmen will be a firm policy and not a wavering policy which fluctuates with the times or swings with the wind, as necessary. I think the country is completely at a loss and will remain at a loss until such time as the minister will make a firm announcement on the trade policy of this government.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot let this opportunity pass without correcting my hon. friend with respect to the statement I made on the setting up of the small business section. There has been no withdrawal from the plan to give such assistance as may be possible to small business in Canada. All I said was that a final decision had not been reached as to whether or not the Department of Trade and Commerce would have that responsibility and I hope within a very short time an announcement will be made to this house as to the setting up of a small business section.

Just on that point, could
the minister indicate on what departmental estimates we might ask about this question of small business, if not on the estimates of his department? What I am getting at is with respect to the remarks of the hon. member for Cartier about the needle trades and about small business, or many small businesses

Supply-Trade and Commerce in that industry. Most of such small businesses would be directly related to the foreign trade of Canada. I do not see, therefore, how we could rule out small business from the trade and commerce estimates if they are related to the foreign trade of the country.
That is all right, but what I was objecting to was dealing with something in anticipation of the supplementary estimates and with items which would concern the setting up of a small business section.

But there is more to it than that, Mr. Chairman. The small businesses being talked about are directly related to the external trade of the country. Surely from that aspect at least they are properly before the committee on this item.
I have sat long enough on the opposition side to know the value of debate and I am not suggesting any restriction of debate whatsoever.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall item 391 carry?

There are many many questions to be answered and I presume the minister intends to answer them on this item. With only a minute or two to go I assume he does not want to open up his answering speech at this time. I do not think therefore that the item can carry.

I have no objection at all to answering questions discussed this afternoon but obviously time does not permit of that tonight. I might, however, take 30 seconds to thank the hon. members who have participated in the debate on the first item. They have shown their interest in the activities of the department and in the expansion of Canada's trade and their comments generally
have been very worth-while. I am even grateful to the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres for depicting me in the light in which I now appear in this House of Commons. It reminds me of the Burns' line, "Oh wad some power the giftie gie us to see oursels as others see us!" I take full note of the alteration that has taken place with my passage from the opposition benches to the government side and I wish the other type of alteration had transpired with my hon. friends who passed from the government benches to the opposition ranks. I wish I could say of them as my hon. friend said of me that when I was sitting there 1 was congenial, easy to get along with and very good natured.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the
house leader what the business is for tomorrow and Saturday?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Tomorrow we shall continue with the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce, then we will take those of the Department of Agriculture, followed by the estimates of the Post Office Department and the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Monday will be private members' day and on Tuesday we plan to commence with item No. 3 on today's order paper, which is the second reading of an act to amend the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, and then item No. 9, which is a resolution concerning the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, and then take the budget resolutions.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
The following answer, deposited with the Clerk of the house, is printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

REPLACEMENT FOR MRS. BIENVENUE
speechtext:
1. Has an appointment been made to replace Mrs. Valmore Bienvenue at the Canadian pavilion of the Brussels universal and international exhibition?
Question
2. If so, (a) what is the name of such person; (b) in what capacity; (c) what are the functions and responsibilities related thereto; (d) what are the qualifications of such person; (e) what salary does the said person receive?
Answer by: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister
of Trade and Commerce):

2.	Answered by No. 1.
